Everything I'm experiencing, all the signals and the monitoring I was telling you about, it's all happening right out in the open, in the physical world, using real people and real events. Well, as I said, the... the real clarity, the moment I knew for a fact what was happening, was about two months ago. Well, um, I mean, I'm still working. I haven't stopped working or anything drastic like that. You can't just walk away from a book of business, especially not in wealth management where people are relying on you for their retirements, their kids' college funds, their estate planning. So, yes, I am absolutely still at my desk, still running the numbers, still doing my job. 

But... if I'm being completely honest with you, and I guess that's the point of all this, my practice has definitely gotten smaller. It’s not a total collapse, but there's a very noticeable contraction. It’s just... it takes so much energy to navigate everything now, you know? 

Like, I find myself missing follow-ups, which is, frankly, a cardinal sin in this industry. Usually, if a client emails me about a portfolio rebalancing question or a sudden market dip, I am back to them within the hour. Absolute maximum. But lately, because I'm so focused on analyzing the signals and trying to figure out who is orchestrating all these coincidences, an email might just sit in my inbox for two days. I get sidetracked. I'll start drafting a reply, and then I'll get caught up trying to cross-reference the client's recent event RSVPs with the people I know are keeping tabs on me, and before I know it, the day is gone and I missed the follow-up entirely. It's embarrassing, really, for someone who prides himself on meticulous service.

And then there are the events. I used to do a lot of public panels—Chamber of Commerce breakfasts, local investment symposiums, real estate market forecasts, that sort of thing. It's essential for networking, great for building the brand and bringing in high-net-worth prospects. But I've started avoiding them completely. I just decline the invitations now. Because standing up there on a stage, with a microphone, knowing that the people tracking me are highly likely to be in the audience, taking notes, analyzing my every word to use in their next signal... it's just too exposed. I feel like a sitting duck up there. So I've pulled back from all those public speaking engagements, which obviously hurts my ability to bring in new clients.

And honestly, just keeping up the same level of day-to-day client contact I used to manage is... it's a massive struggle. I used to do quarterly lunches with all my top-tier clients, plus monthly check-in calls just to shoot the breeze and talk about market trends. Now, I find myself pushing those calls back, rescheduling them, or just sending a quick, generic email instead of picking up the phone. It's not that I don't care about their portfolios—I do, deeply—but the mental bandwidth required to have a normal, relaxed conversation about municipal bonds while simultaneously scanning their words for hidden messages or trying to figure out if they've inadvertently been compromised by the people watching me... it's exhausting. It just drains you. 

So, yeah, I'm still functioning, I'm still a licensed advisor, but the actual scope of what I can handle, the size of my practice... it has definitely shrunk because I just can't juggle the normal demands of the job alongside everything else that's going on.

Well, sleep... no, actually. You would think so, right? Given the profound exhaustion I was just describing to you. You'd logically assume that with my battery constantly at one percent, I'd be sleeping fourteen hours a day, or conversely, that the stress of the... the monitoring and the signals would keep me up all night, just staring at the ceiling and analyzing everything. And that really hasn't changed at all. Not over the last two years since that nonprofit dinner, and not over the last couple of months with everything else going on. 

I put my head on the pillow, and I'm usually out within ten or fifteen minutes. I don't toss and turn, I don't wake up at 3:00 AM with my mind racing. I mean, occasionally I might get up for a glass of water, but nothing out of the ordinary, and I go right back to sleep. And I definitely don't sleep the day away. 

The issue isn't the sleep itself. I'm getting my seven-plus hours, mechanically speaking. The problem is that when that alarm goes off at 6:15, I don't feel refreshed. I still feel that heavy, molasses feeling I was telling you about. I'll just lie there for twenty minutes, looking at the ceiling, knowing I have a completely solid, uninterrupted night of sleep in the bank, but feeling like I haven't slept in a year. So the sleep is happening exactly like it's supposed to. It's just... it's like plugging a broken phone into a charger all night. The charger is working fine, the outlet is fine, the power is flowing, but the battery itself just won't hold the charge anymore. So, no, to answer your question, no changes in the actual sleep itself.
